newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem president holds big lead in Bosnia vote.
newsitem.headline: Moslem president holds big lead in Bosnia vote.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic neared victory on Tuesday in elections for a new inter-ethnic presidency which were hoisting wartime hardliners back into power with large majorities.

Izetbegovic, Momcilo Krajisnik of the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croat candidate Kresimir Zubak -- all nationalists -- staked out unbeatable leads over moderate rivals for the presidency's three seats.

But the main Serb opposition leader came from nowhere to score almost half as many votes as Krajisnik, confirming a backlash against Serb ultra-nationalists who tore Bosnia apart and got rich in war while most compatriots sank into penury.

Despite Krajisnik's reputation as a hard-line separatist, Western diplomats and Bosnian Serb sources said they expected him to cooperate in a new power-sharing arrangement designed to reintegrate Bosnia after 43 months of war.
With about 80 percent of the votes tallied, Izetbegovic had 629,439 votes compared with 508,026 for Krajisnik, speaker of parliament in the current Serb entity of Bosnia.
Although the joint three-member Bosnian presidency must govern by consensus, the candidate which wins the most votes will be declared chairman, and represent the country abroad.
Krajisnik may well have been knocked out of the running for chairman by the surprisingly strong performance of top rival Mladen Ivanic, who weighed in with more than 240,000 votes.
Izetbegovic's main challenger, former prime minister Haris Silajdzic, had only 110,845 votes.

Robert Frowick, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's mission in Bosnia which supervised the elections, said final results for the presidency race would be announced on Wednesday.
The outcome of parallel voting for an inter-ethnic Bosnian parliament was not expected until later this week.

Diplomats said Izetbegovic looked capable of fending off any late surge by Krajisnik because Moslems outnumbered Serbs in the electorate and because Silajdzic had fared worse than widely predicted, averting a split of Moslem votes.
In the race for the Croat slot in the presidency, Zubak was cruising to victory. His only challenger had around 10 percent.
Under the Dayton agreement, the three-man executive will lead Bosnia for two years, governing by consensus.

Critics say that could be a recipe for government gridlock. Krajisnik's Serb Semocratic Party (SDS) waged a blatant pro- independence election campaign, flouting commitments to unity enshrined in the Dayton treaty text.
But U.S. envoys used the threat of indefinite international sanctions to wring pledges from SDS leaders last week to join Moslems and Croats in a federal governing structure.
Izetbegovic's SDA party, though Moslem nationalist in tone, professes support for restoring a tolerant multi-ethnic Bosnia.
Mirza Hajric, a spokesman in Bosnia's outgoing Moslem-led republic government, said it was confident U.S. pressure on the Serbs would ensure joint government got off the ground.
The United States said it would work with Bosnia's election victors over the next month or so, to set up joint governing bodies and then decide whether NATO forces should remain.
A 53,000-strong NATO-led force separated and demobilised Bosnia's factional armies early this year in a key pre-election step mandated by the Dayton treaty.

A team of OSCE-affiliated international observers has pronounced the elections free of serious irregularities in a preliminary report expected to lead to certification of the vote by Frowick later this month.

But the observers urged the OSCE not to hold municipal elections in November as planned until problems with rigged voter lists on Serb territory are solved and drastic curbs on free movement across ethnic lines are lifted.
